newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistanis flay Gujral "somersault" on Kashmir.
newsitem.headline: Pakistanis flay Gujral "somersault" on Kashmir.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's about turn on peace talks with Kashmiri militants ran into Pakistani criticism on Monday.
Analysts in Islamabad said the move appeared to be an attempt by New Delhi to buy time.

"This somersault is nothing new because the Indian leaders have never translated their words into any serious action," Agha Murtaza Pooya, a former head of the Islamabad-based Institute of Strategic Studies, told Reuters.

On Saturday Gujral had offered unconditional talks with militants during a visit to the Indian-ruled part of the disputed Himalayan region of Jammu and Kashmir state, but on Sunday he asked them to lay down their arms before talks to end a seven-year-old rebellion in the state could begin.
No comment was immediately available from the government of Pakistan, which controls one-third of the state and questions the legitimacy of the Indian rule in the region.
"Gujral has tried to go down there ... to assuage them by telling them 'Okay we are prepared for talks' (but) he has also withdrawn the ... offer by asking for abject surrender," Pooya said.
"It is leading nowhere. The Indians are just trying to make a sweet symphony ... while continuing to intensify their barbarities in occupied Kashmir."
"This does not look good when he (Gujral) contradicts himself," said Ghani Jafar, a research analyst at the Islamabad-based Regional Institute of Strategic Studies.
"But to my understanding this is just a manifestation of the larger problem which India is faced with today with reference to Kashmir," he added.
He said India felt compelled to find a political settlement because of international expectations on New Dehli, but in reality it wanted to time to crush the militants.

"There is considerable international expectation for India to find a political settlement for which negotiations with people in Kashmir are an essential part," Jafar said. "On the other hand, they wish to crush the struggle and buy time without engaging in meaningful dialogue with Kashmiris and Pakistan."
Dozens of guerrilla groups have been involved in hostilities since 1990, seeking either Kashmir's merger with Pakistan or independence.
India and Pakistan have fought two of their three wars over Kashmir since independence from Britain in 1947, and more than 20,000 people have died in the violence in Indian Kashmir.
India accuses Pakistan of arming Kashmiri militants, but Pakistan says it provides only moral and diplomatic support.
